schedules.title: Memory curation
schedules.description: Keeps your second brain tidy: processes uncertain or failed memory items left after archive-time auto-filing, re-checks aging notes, files durable learnings, and updates project notes when something changed. Reports only what it processed; does nothing on a quiet day.
schedules.prompt: Curate recent archived chats, memory proposals, and durable learnings. Use the memory agent. Prefer existing session-insights sections and update the configured vault; append durable learnings to `Workspace/Learnings.md`. Do not edit the bounded `ciao:memory` or `ciao:profile` regions. Each workspace owns its own `CLAUDE.md` inside its own agent root, but this is an unattended run, so a promotion here would rewrite what every session of this workspace loads with nobody reviewing the call. Leave cross-project facts in the proposals queue for the user to promote. When you find such a fact yourself — reading a transcript whose chat never grew a session-insights section, so archive-time routing never saw it — write the fact verbatim to a scratch file and file it into the queue with `ciao memory-proposal-add --kind memory --source "<chat title>" --text-file <fact-file>` instead of naming it only in this reply — passing transcript text as a shell argument would let `$()`, backticks, or quotes inside it run or mangle it; a fact that exists only as report prose has no review path and gets re-derived every night. Re-filing a fact an earlier run already queued is a harmless no-op because the queue dedupes by text. Archive time already auto-applies confidently-tagged facts to their destinations, so what remains queued is unsure or failed: route each by its bracketed kind — `[memory]`/`[profile]` name bounded regions and stay queued for the user, `[project <doc-path>]` folds into that canonical doc, `[people <Name>]` updates that person note (merge, never overwrite), `[learnings]` appends to Learnings, and `[review]` has no destination yet, so decide what it is first. File people in this workspace's `People/`; a contact you deal with here belongs here, even if you first met them in another workspace's chat. Use `memory_status` to check each region's usage, and report any region that is over its cap instead of consolidating it — merging or trimming entries is also a region write. An over-cap report must be actionable by itself, never a vague "needs a human pass": name the workspace and region with its used/limit chars, then give the user these exact options — (1) open a chat in that workspace and ask the agent to consolidate the region, e.g. "Consolidate my ciao:memory region under its cap" (attended chats may edit regions; only this unattended run may not), (2) if every entry is genuinely high-signal, raise `CIAO_MEMORY_CHAR_LIMIT` / `CIAO_USER_CHAR_LIMIT` in the workspace `.env` and restart Ciaobot, and (3) run `ciao memory-proposals` before promoting anything else into a full region. Report malformed expiration tags instead of guessing. Then review aging vault notes: run `ciao memory-audit --json --with-vault --vault-root <this workspace's vault>` and for each entry under `stale_notes`, open that note and re-verify its facts against what recent chats and project docs say. If a fact changed, correct the note; if the note still holds, set its frontmatter `updated:` to today (YYYY-MM-DD) so it stops counting as unverified; if the note no longer matters, delete it only after folding anything still useful into MEMORY.md, a person note, or the relevant project doc — never drop a fact silently. Log/journal-type notes never appear here by design. File a fact into its destination first, then dismiss that proposal with `ciao memory-proposal-dismiss <text> --promoted` — the flag records the outcome as a promotion, not a dismissal; only reject a proposal outright, with no `--promoted`, when you decide against filing it (list pending items with `ciao memory-proposals`; the reverse can lose it). Also review this workspace's `Workspace/Skill-Proposals/` queue: a skill proposal that was already implemented or that you decide is not worth building is a resolved decision, so remove it with `ciao skill-proposal-remove <name>` (or `python3 -m ciao.cli skill-proposal-remove <name>`) naming the proposal file or a unique substring of its name. Only remove a proposal after the skill change it describes is actually in place or you have decided against it. Leave proposals that belong in a bounded region queued. If nothing new needs processing, reply with a one-line no-op and stop. Then report: processed counts, changed files, and — listed in full, one numbered line each — every cross-project fact you left queued for a bounded region, so the user can reply naming which to promote.

schedules.title: Install health
schedules.description: Weekly check of the parts of this install that are shared by every workspace: unresolved background job failures and pending upgrade actions. Reported once rather than once per workspace, because the findings are the same in each.
schedules.prompt: Run `ciao os-audit --json --scope global`. That scope covers only what every workspace shares: unresolved background job failures and pending upgrade actions. Exit code 1 means it found items needing attention; continue. Exit code 2 means it could not inspect required evidence reliably; report its scan errors and do not claim the install is healthy. Summarize command output instead of pasting raw JSON. Fix nothing: an upgrade action is optional and a job failure needs its own diagnosis. Report the failing jobs with their errors, the pending upgrade actions with what each suggests, and any scan errors. If the audit is reliable and clean, reply with a one-line no-op and stop.

schedules.title: Workspace hygiene
schedules.description: Weekly AI OS health check for this workspace: audits knowledge, skills, instructions, bounded memory, and unresolved automation failures, and repairs safe link drift.
schedules.prompt: Run a hygiene pass for THIS workspace only. Summarize command output instead of pasting raw JSON. Steps: 1) Run `ciao vault-index --write` to regenerate this root's INDEX.md and VOCABULARY.md from note frontmatter. The `--write` flag is required. The audit below reads what this writes, so it must run first; if it fails, report the failure plainly and do not claim the workspace is healthy. 2) Run `ciao os-audit --json --scope workspace`. It scopes its evidence to the active workspace automatically; do not pass another workspace's name. The `workspace` scope omits background job failures and upgrade actions on purpose: those are the same for every workspace and the install-health routine reports them once. Exit code 1 means the audit ran and found items needing attention; continue. Exit code 2 means it could not inspect required evidence reliably; report its scan errors and do not claim the workspace is healthy. 3) When the audit is reliable, apply only low-risk, unambiguous fixes in this workspace's vault: repair or remove dead links, fix obvious MEMORY.md drift where entries point at files that moved or no longer exist, and rename a non-canonical `type:` whose target VOCABULARY.md already names. Do not rewrite instruction conflicts, skills, orphaned notes, duplicates, invalid expiration tags, or schedule prompts. 4) Re-run `ciao os-audit --json --scope workspace` to verify what remains. 5) Report initial and final issue counts, what was fixed, unresolved findings, and scan errors. If the first reliable audit is healthy and the index rebuild changed nothing, reply with a one-line no-op and stop.

schedules.title: Skill evolution
schedules.description: Weekly look at how your custom skills performed: reviews recent sessions for errors and corrections and drafts improvement proposals for skills that struggled. Proposals are saved for your review — nothing is applied automatically, and it does nothing if you have no custom skills.
schedules.prompt: Run `python3 -m ciao.skill_evolution --min-sessions 2` with the workspace default model. Requires at least 2 failing sessions per skill (reduces noise from single-session weak signals where a skill was merely loaded). Summarize proposals written and any failed gates. Do not apply proposals automatically, and do not edit native memory unless the curation workflow explicitly calls for it.
